definition: He breathed: (S, A, K:) said of a man, (A,) and of a horse.
sourceDefinition: He breathed: (S, A, K:) said of a man, (A,) and of a horse. (S.) ― -b2- [ It emitted an odour: ] it (a thing, Msb) stank; (S, Msb, K;) as also A^arowaHa : (Msb, TA:) the former said of flesh-meat, (S, K,) and of water; (K;) and so the latter: (TA:) or the latter, it became altered [ for the worse ] in odour; (Lh, S, M, A, Msb;) said of flesh-meat, (Lh, M, A, * Msb,) and of water, (Lh, S, M, A, Msb,) &c.; (S;) and so the former, said of water: (L, TA:) ISd makes a distinction between ArwH and ↓ trw~H [q. v., as does also J,] said of water. (Msb, TA.) ― -b3- Also, (inf. n. A_iraAHapN , L,) He (a man, S, and a beast, Lh) revived, or his spirit returned to him, after fatigue; (Lh, S, K;) like ↓ AstrAH , q. v.: (TA:) and he had rest. (K.) ― -b4- And [hence], (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. A_iraAHapN , (TA,) or A_irowaAHN , (Msb,) (assumed tropical:) He (a man) died; (S, Msb, K;) as though he found rest: and he (a camel) died, or perished. (TA.) You say, A^araAHa faA^araAHa [ He rested, i. e. had rest, and so rested others], meaning (assumed tropical:) he died, and so people became at rest from him. (A.) ― -b5- [Hence also,] A^araHonaA biAlS~alaApi We performed the act of prayer: because its performance is [a cause of] rest to the soul; the waiting for the time thereof being troublesome. (Msb.) ― -b6- A^araAHato said of camels &c. [as though meaning They returned in the evening, or afternoon, to rest ]: see 1, in the latter half of the paragraph. ― -b7- ArAH , inf. n. A_iraAHapN and A_iraAHN , said of a man, His camels, and sheep or goats, and cattle, returned to him in the evening, or afternoon, from pasture. (L.) ― -b8- And ArAH , [app. for ArAH baEiyrahu ,] like wise said of a man, He alighted from his camel to rest him and to alleviate him. (L.) ― -b9- A^araAHuwA , or A^arowaHuwA : see 1, in the last quarter of the paragraph. -A2- A^araAHahu and A^arowaHahu , and ArAH Alr~iyHa , &c.: see 1, in the last quarter of the paragraph, in twelve places. ― -b2- ArAHhu , (S, A, Msb, K,) inf. n. A_iraAHapN , (Msb, TA,) and ↓ raAHapN is a subst. used as an inf. n., [i. e. a quasi-inf. n.,] like TaAEapN and EaArapN used as inf. ns. of A^aTaAEahu and A^aEaArahu , (TA,) said of God, (S, K,) or of a man, (A, Msb,) He rested him, made him to be at rest or at ease, or gave him rest; (S, * A, * Msb;) namely, a hired man, (Msb,) or any man; as also Eanohu ↓ rw~H : (TA:) and the former, He (God) caused him to enter into a state of rest, (K, TA,) or of mercy. (TA.) And binaA ↓ raw~iHuwA (K in art. lv ) Give ye us rest. (TK in that art.) And ArAH baEiyrahu He revived, or recovered, his camel. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] ArAH Aln~aAsa biAlS~alaApi He chanted the call to prayer, and so made the people to ease their hearts by performing the act of prayer. (L.) ― -b4- And ArAH , (S, M, A, Msb, K,) inf. n. A_iraAHapN ; (M, Mgh;) accord. to one dial., haraAHa , aor. yuhariyHu ; (TA;) and ↓ rw~H , (S, * A, TA,) inf. n. tarowiyHN ; (S;) He (the pastor, Msb) drove back, or brought back, (S, M, Msb, K,) camels, (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) and sheep or goats, (M, A, * Mgh,) and cows or bulls, (A, * Mgh,) in the evening, or afternoon, (M, Msb,) after the declining of the sun from the meridian, (S,) [ from their place of pasture, ] to their nightly resting-place, (S, M, K,) or A_ilaY A^aholihaA [and EalaY A^aholihaA (for you say raAHato EalaY A^aholihaA ) i. e. to their owners ]. (Msb.) ― -b5- [Hence,] ArAH Ealayohi Haq~ahu (assumed tropical:) He restored to him his right, or due; (S, K;) as also A^arowaHa . (K.) And the saying, in a trad., of Umm-Zara, ArAH EalaY~a naEamFA variy~FA (assumed tropical:) He gave me much cattle: because she was [as though she were] a muraAH for his bounty. (L.)

definition: The soul, spirit, or vital principle;
sourceDefinition: The soul, spirit, or vital principle; syn. nafosN ; (IAar, IAmb, L, Msb, TA, and S and K &c. in art. nfs ; [but there is a difference between these two words, for they are not always interchangeable, as I have shown in art. nfs ;]) [i. e.] maA bihi HayaApu AlA^anofusi ; (K; [see also rawoHN , third sentence;]) often occurring in the Kur and the Traditions in different senses, but generally signifying [as explained above, i. e.] the vital principle; (IAth, TA;) [or the nervous fluid; or animal spirit; ] a subtile vaporous substance, which is the principle of vitality and of sensation and of voluntary motion; also called the ruwH HayawaAniY~ ; (KT in explanation of the term nafosN ;) or a subtile body, the source of which is the hollow of the corporeal heart, and which diffuses itself into all the other parts of the body by means of the pulsing veins, or arteries: (KT in explanation of the term Alr~uwHu AlHayawaAniY~u : [so too nafosN ; q. v.: see also Gen. ix. 4: many of the ancients believed the soul to reside in the blood: see Aristotle, De Anim. i. 2, and Virgil's Æn. ix. 349:]) or the vital principle in man: (Fr, TA:) or the breath which a man breathes, and which pervades the whole body: [and this seems to be the original idea expressed by the word:] after its exit, he ceases to breathe; and when it has completely gone forth, his eyes remain gazing towards it until they close; called in Pers. jaAno : (AHeyth, TA:) accord. to the Sunnees, the rational soul, ( Aln~afosu Aln~aATiqapu , [also termed Alr~uwHu AlA_inosaAniY~u ,]) which is adapted to the faculty of making known its ideas by means of speech, and of understanding speech, and which perishes not with the perishing of the body, being a substance, not an accident; as is shown by the words in the Kur iii. 163, which refer to the rwH : (Msb:) most of the doctors of the fundamentals of religion forbid the diving into this matter, because God has abstained from making it known: (TA:) the philosophers say that it is the blood, by the exhausting of which the life ceases: (Msb:) the word is masc., (IAar, IAmb, Az, S, M, A, Msb, K, *) thus, with the Arabs, differing from nafosN , for this they make fem., (IAar, IAmb, Msb,) but the former is also fem., (S, M, A, Msb, K,) app. as meaning nafosN , (Msb,) as is said in the R; (TA;) and most hold it to be as often fem. as it is masc.: (MF:) one says xaraja ruwHuhu (IAar, Az, TA) [and also xarajato ruwHuhu , meaning His soul departed, or went forth ]: the pl. is A^arowaAHN . (S, Msb.) ― -b2- Also i. q. nafoxN (K) [properly A blowing with the mouth; but here] meaning wind that issues from the ruwH ; (TA;) wind, or breath. (ADk, TA.) Dhu-r-Rummeh says, respecting fire that he had struck, and upon which he bade his companion to blow, A^aHoyihaA biruwHika Give life to it, or enliven it, with thy wind [or breath ]. (TA.) And one says, malaA^a Alqirobapa mino ruwHihi He filled the skin with his wind; with his breath. (ADk, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] Alr~uwHu also signifies (assumed tropical:) Inspiration, or divine revelation; (Zj, Th, K;) such as is imparted by means of an angel: thus in the Kur xvi. 2 and xl. 15: so called because it quickens from the death of infidelity, and thus is, to a man, like the ruwH which is the vital principle of his body: (T:) or (so says Zj accord. to the L, but in the K “ and ” ) the prophetic commission. (Zj, K.) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) The Kur-án; (IAar, Zj, S, * A, * K;) whereby God's creatures are [spiritually] quickened, and guided to the right way. (TA.) So in the trad., taHaAyawoA bi*ikori A@ll~`hi wa ruwHihi (tropical:) [ Revive yourselves with God's book of religion and religious laws, (or *ikor may here have some other meaning,) and his Kur-án ]. (TA. [Mentioned also in the A; in a copy of which, in the place of taHaAyawoA , I find taHaAbuwA , an evident mistranscription.]) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) What God ordains and commands (K, TA) by means of his assistants and angels. (TA.) ― -b6- Also Jibreel [i. e. Gabriel ]; (S, * A, * K;) called in the Kur [xxvi. 193] Alr~uwHu AlA^amiynu , and [in ii. 81] ruwHu Alqudusi or Alqudosi , as related by Az on the authority of Th. (TA.) [The last of these appellations, or generally, but incorrectly, Alr~uwHu Alqudusu , is applied by the Eastern Christians among the Arabs to The Holy Spirit; the Third Person of the Trinity. ] ― -b7- And [sometimes Our Lord ] Jesus. (S, * A, * K.) ― -b8- And A certain angel, (I'Ab, K,) in the Seventh Heaven, (I'Ab, TA,) whose face is like that of a man, and his body like that of the [ other ] angels: (I'Ab, K:) or certain creatures resembling mankind, but not men: so in the Kur lxxviii. 38: (Zj:) or the watchers over the angels who are watchers over the sons of Adam, whose faces are said to be like the faces of men, and whom the other angels see not, like as we see not the watchers nor the [ other ] angels. (Th.) ― -b9- See also rawoHN , in three places. -A2- Also pl. of raw^uwHN : (L:) ― -b2- and of A^arowaHu . (S &c.)

Dhu-r-Rummeh says, respecting fire that he had struck, and upon which he bade his companion to blow, A^aHoyihaA biruwHika Give life to it, or enliven it, with thy wind [or breath ]. (TA.) And one says, malaA^a Alqirobapa mino ruwHihi He filled the skin with his wind; with his breath. (ADk, TA.)

[Hence,] Alr~uwHu also signifies (assumed tropical:) Inspiration, or divine revelation; (Zj, Th, K;) such as is imparted by means of an angel: thus in the Kur xvi. 2 and xl. 15: so called because it quickens from the death of infidelity, and thus is, to a man, like the ruwH which is the vital principle of his body: (T:) or (so says Zj accord. to the L, but in the K “ and ” ) the prophetic commission. (Zj, K.)

And (assumed tropical:) The Kur-án; (IAar, Zj, S, * A, * K;) whereby God's creatures are [spiritually] quickened, and guided to the right way. (TA.) So in the trad., taHaAyawoA bi*ikori A@ll~`hi wa ruwHihi (tropical:) [ Revive yourselves with God's book of religion and religious laws, (or *ikor may here have some other meaning,) and his Kur-án ]. (TA. [Mentioned also in the A; in a copy of which, in the place of taHaAyawoA , I find taHaAbuwA , an evident mistranscription.])
And (assumed tropical:) What God ordains and commands (K, TA) by means of his assistants and angels. (TA.)

or animal spirit; ] a subtile vaporous substance, which is the principle of vitality and of sensation and of voluntary motion; also called the ruwH HayawaAniY~ ; (KT in explanation of the term nafosN ;) or a subtile body, the source of which is the hollow of the corporeal heart, and which diffuses itself into all the other parts of the body by means of the pulsing veins, or arteries: (KT in explanation of the term Alr~uwHu AlHayawaAniY~u : [so too nafosN ; q. v.: see also Gen. ix. 4: many of the ancients believed the soul to reside in the blood: see Aristotle, De Anim. i. 2, and Virgil's Æn. ix. 349:]) or the vital principle in man: (Fr, TA:) or the breath which a man breathes, and which pervades the whole body: [and this seems to be the original idea expressed by the word:] after its exit, he ceases to breathe; and when it has completely gone forth, his eyes remain gazing towards it until they close; called in Pers. jaAno : (AHeyth, TA:) accord. to the Sunnees, the rational soul, ( Aln~afosu Aln~aATiqapu , [also termed Alr~uwHu AlA_inosaAniY~u ,]) which is adapted to the faculty of making known its ideas by means of speech, and of understanding speech, and which perishes not with the perishing of the body, being a substance, not an accident; as is shown by the words in the Kur iii. 163, which refer to the rwH : (Msb:) most of the doctors of the fundamentals of religion forbid the diving into this matter, because God has abstained from making it known: (TA:) the philosophers say that it is the blood, by the exhausting of which the life ceases: (Msb:) the word is masc., (IAar, IAmb, Az, S, M, A, Msb, K, *) thus, with the Arabs, differing from nafosN , for this they make fem., (IAar, IAmb, Msb,) but the former is also fem., (S, M, A, Msb, K,) app. as meaning nafosN , (Msb,) as is said in the R; (TA.) ― -b6- Also Jibreel [i. e. Gabriel ]; (S, * A, * K;) called in the Kur [xxvi. 193] Alr~uwHu AlA^amiynu , and [in ii. 81] ruwHu Alqudusi or Alqudosi , as related by Az on the authority of Th. (TA.) [The last of these appellations, or generally, but incorrectly, Alr~uwHu Alqudusu , is applied by the Eastern Christians among the Arabs to The Holy Spirit; the Third Person of the Trinity. ] ― -b7- And [sometimes Our Lord ] Jesus. (S, * A, * K.) ― -b8- And A certain angel, (I'Ab, K,) in the Seventh Heaven, (I'Ab, TA,) whose face is like that of a man, and his body like that of the [ other ] angels: (I'Ab, K:) or certain creatures resembling mankind, but not men: so in the Kur lxxviii. 38: (Zj:) or the watchers over the angels who are watchers over the sons of Adam, whose faces are said to be like the faces of men, and whom the other angels see not, like as we see not the watchers nor the [ other ] angels. (Th.) ― -b9- See also rawoHN , in three places. -A2- Also pl. of raw^uwHN : (L:) ― -b2- and of A^arowaHu . (S &c.)

(TA.) ― -b2- And [particularly] Width, or wideness, in the space between the thighs: (TA:) or width, or wideness, (S, Mgh, K,) in, (S, K,) or of, (Mgh,) [or between, ] the two legs, (S, Mgh, K,) less than what is termed faHajN , (S, K,) or less than fajajN , (A, Mgh,) with wideness between the fore parts of the feet, and nearness of the heels, each to the other: (S:) or [simply] wideness between the fore parts of the feet, and nearness of the heels, each to the other: (Msb:) or a spreading in the fore part of each foot: (Lth, Mgh, Msb:) or a turning over of the foot upon its outer side: IAar says that rawaHN in the legs is less than fadaEN , and this is less than EaqalN . (TA.) -A3- h`*aA AlA^amoru bayonanaA rawaHN means This is a thing, or an affair, which we do by turns; as also EawarN . (TA.)

definition: originally riwoHN , the w being changed into Y because of the preceding kesreh, (T, S, Msb,) as is shown by its dim.
sourceDefinition: originally riwoHN , the w being changed into Y because of the preceding kesreh, (T, S, Msb,) as is shown by its dim. mentioned below; (T, Msb;) Sb held it to be of the measure fiEolN ; and Abu-l-Hasan, fiEolN and fuEolN ; [if the latter, originally ruyoHN ;] (TA;) [ Wind; i. e.] the air that is made to obey [ the will of God ] and to run its course between heaven and earth: (Msb, TA:) or the breath ( nasiym ) of the air; and in like manner, of anything: (L, TA:) said to be thus called because it generally brings rawoH and raAHap [i. e. rest, or ease]: (IAmb, MF:) one says riyHN and ↓ riyHapN , like daArN and daArapN ; (S;) [using the latter as a more special term; for] riyHapN signifies a portion of wind ( TaAy^ifapN mino riyHK ) [meaning a wind of short duration; or a breath, puff, blast, or gust, of wind ]; (Sb, M;) but riyHN and ↓ riyHapN may be used in the same sense; i. e. the latter may be used as syn. with the former, and they are mentioned by some [as analogous] with kawokabN and kawokabapN : (Sb, L:) riyoH is of the fem. gender (IAmb, L, Msb) in most cases; (Msb;) and all the other names for wind are fem. except A_iEoSaArN , which is masc.; (IAmb, Msb;) but ryH is sometimes made masc. as meaning hawaA='N : (AZ, Msb:) [it is used by physicians as signifying flatus, flatuosity, or flatulence; as in the phrase riyHN galiyZapN a gross flatus: ] the pl. [of pauc.] is A^arowaAHN (S, Mgh, Msb, K, &c.) and A^aroyaAHN , (S, Msb, K,) the latter used by some, but disallowed by AHát because there is in it no kesreh to cause the w to be changed into Y , (L, Msb,) and [the pl. of mult. is] riyaAHN , (S, Mgh, Msb, K, &c.,) with Y because of the kesreh, (Msb,) and riyaHN ; (K, but not found by SM in any other lexicon;) and the pl. pl. is A^araAwiyHu [pl. of A^arowaAHN ] and A^araAyiyHu [pl. of A^aroyaAHN ]: (K:) the dim. of riyHN is ↓ ruwayoHapN . (T, Msb.) riyaAHN , or another form of pl., is often used in a good sense; and the sing., in an evil sense; because the Arabs say that the clouds are not made to give rain save by diverse winds blowing together; and this distinction is observed in the Kur-án. (L.) Hence, it is related in a trad., that he [Mohammad] used to say, when wind rose, Aall~`hum~a A@joEalohaA riyaAHFA wa laA tajoEalohaA riyHFA [ O God, make it to be winds, and made it not to be a wind ]. (TA.) [But this distinction is not always observed.] One says, fulaAnN yamiylu maEa kul~i riyHK (tropical:) [ Such a one inclines, or turns, with every wind ]. (TA.) And fulaAnN kaAlr~iyHi Almurosalapi [ Such a one is like the wind that is sent forth to drive the clouds, and produce rain; (see the Kur xxv. 50;)] meaning, (tropical:) quick, or prompt, to do acts of kindness, or beneficence. (A.) And rajulN saAkinu Alr~iyHi (tropical:) A man who is calm, sedate, staid, or grave. (A.) ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) Predominance, or prevalence; and power, or force. (S, K.) A poet says, (S,) namely, Suleyk Ibn-Es-Sulakeh, or Taäbbata-Sharrà, or Aashà of the tribe of Fahm, (TA, and so in one of my copies of the S,) A^atanoZuraAni qaliylFA rayova gafolatihimo A^awo taEoduwaAni faA_in~a Alr~iyHa liloEaAdiY (assumed tropical:) [ Will ye two await, a little, the time of their inadvertence, or will ye act aggressively? for prevalence is for the aggressor ]. (S.) And hence the phrase in the Kur [viii. 48], wa ta*ohaba riyHukumo (assumed tropical:) [ And your predominance, or power, depart ]: (S:) [or in this latter instance it has the meaning next following.] ― -b3- (tropical:) Aid against an enemy; or victory, or conquest: (K, TA:) and (tropical:) a turn of good fortune. (A, K, TA.) One says, *ahabato riyHuhumo (tropical:) Their turn of good fortune departed. (A.) And A_i*aA hab~ato riyaAHuka faA@gotanimohaA (tropical:) [ When thy turns of good fortune come, avail thyself of them ]. (A.) And Alr~iyHu liA=li fulaAnK (tropical:) Aid against the enemy, or victory or conquest, or the turn of good fortune, is to the family of such a one. (TA.) ― -b4- See also rawoHN . ― -b5- And see raAy^iHapN (with which it is syn.), in four places. ― -b6- Also (assumed tropical:) A good, sweet, or pleasant, thing. (K.) ― -b7- The pl. A^arowaAHN occurs in a trad. as meaning (tropical:) The jinn, or genii; because they are [supposed to be often] invisible, like the wind. (TA.)

definition: Rest, repose, or ease;
sourceDefinition: Rest, repose, or ease; contr. of taEabN ; (TA;) cessation of trouble, or inconvenience, and of toil, or fatigue; (Msb;) [or freedom therefrom; ] and ↓ rawoHN signifies the same as raAHapN , (S, A, K,) from AlAisotiraAHapu ; (S, A;) like ↓ rawaAHN [mentioned in the first paragraph as an inf. n. in a similar sense, as are also raAHapN and ↓ rawoHapN and ↓ rawaAHapN and ↓ rawiyHapN , i. e., as meaning the experiencing relief from grief &c.]. (TA.) You say, ↓ maA lifulaAnK fiY h`*aA AlA^amori mino rawaAHK i. e. raAHapK [ There is not, for such a one, in this affair, or case, or event, any rest, &c.]. (TA.) And AifoEalo ↓ *`lika fiY saraAHK wa rawaAHK (tropical:) Do thou that in a state of ease (S, A, K) and rest. (A.) ― -b2- See also 4, near the middle of the paragraph. -A2- (assumed tropical:) A wife; syn. EirosN : (K:) because one trusts to her, or relies upon her, and becomes quiet, or easy, in mind. (TA.) -A3- The hand; syn. kaf~N : (S, K:) or [rather] the palm of the hand; (Msb, MF;) for the term kaf~ includes the rAHp with the fingers: (MF:) pl. ↓ raAHN , (S, A, * Msb, K, *) [or rather this, said in the K to be syn. with raAHaAtN , is a coll. gen. n., of which raAHapN is the n. un.,] and [the pl. is] raAHaAtN . (Msb, K.) You say, dafaEuwhu ↓ biAlr~aAHi [ They pushed him with the palms of the hands ]. (A.) The saying of a poet, ↓ A_i*aA dalakato $amosu Aln~ahaAri biraAHi is explained as meaning When the sun of day has set, and men, looking towards it, shield themselves from its rays with the palms of their hands: or, accord. to IAar, when the [ sun of ] day has become dark, by reason of the dust of battle, and it is as though it were setting, and people have found rest from its heat. (L. [See also baraAHN , in art. brH ; where other readings are mentioned.]) ― -b2- [Hence, app., as seems to be indicated in the TA,] raAHapu Alkalobi (tropical:) A certain plant. (K, TA.) ― -b3- And *uw Alr~aAHapi (assumed tropical:) A sword of El-Mukhtár Ibn-Abee-' Obeyd (K, TA) Eth-Thakafee. (TA.) ― -b4- raAHapN also signifies A court, an open area, or a yard, (K, TA,) of a house. (TA.) One says, tarakotuhu A^anoqaY mina Alr~aAHapi (K, TA) i. e. I left him, or it, more clear than the court, open area, or yard, [of a house,] or than the palm of the hand; (TA;) meaning, (assumed tropical:) without anything. definition: a word respecting the formation of which there are different opinions;
sourceDefinition: a word respecting the formation of which there are different opinions; many saying that its medial radical letter is w , and its original form rayowaHaAnN , as may be argued from the form of its dim., mentioned below; (Msb;) others, that its original form is rawoyaHaAnN ; (MF;) and others, that its medial radical letter is Y , and that it is of the same measure as $ayoTaAnN , as may be argued from the form of its pl., mentioned below; (Msb;) A certain plant, (S, K,) well known, (S,) of sweet odour; (K;) the $aAhasofaram [or $aAhisofaram , i. e. basil-royal, or common sweet basil, ocimum basilicum, the seed of which (called bizoru Alr~ayoHaAni ) is used in medicine]: (Mgh: [see also HabaqN :]) or any sweet-smelling plant; (T, Mgh, Msb, K;) but when used absolutely by the vulgar, a particular plant [that mentioned above] is meant thereby: (Msb:) or the extremities thereof; (K;) i. e. the extremities of any sweet-smelling herb, when the first of its blossoms come forth upon it: (TA:) or the leaves thereof: (K:) or the leaves of seed-produce: so, accord. to Fr, in the Kur lv. 11: (S, TA:) [it is a coll. gen. n.:] the n. un. is with p ; (TA;) and is applied to a bunch ( TaAqapN ) of rayoHaAn ; and, with the article Al , (as a proper name, TA,) the Hanowap [a certain plant respecting which authors differ]: (K:) the dim. of rayoHaAnN is ruwayoHiynN : (Msb:) and the pl. is rayaAHiynu . (Mgh, Msb) rayoHaAnu AlHabaAHimi : and rayoHaAnu Al$~uyuwxi : see HabaqN . rayoHaAnu Alqubuwri is a name of The mirosiyn [or myrtle-tree ]. (TA in art. mrs .) ― -b2- (tropical:) Offspring; (L, K, TA;) from the same word as signifying “ any sweet-smelling plant; (Ham p. 713;) or from the same word in the sense next following: (L:) [a coll. gen. n.: n. un. with p ; whence,] riyoHaAnanaY~a [meaning (tropical:) My two descendants ] occurs in a saying of Mohammad as applied to El-Hasan and El-Hoseyn. (TA.) ― -b3- (tropical:) A bounty, or gift, of God; such as the means of subsistence, &c.; syn. rizoqN : (S, L, K, TA:) said to be of the dial. of Himyer. (MF.) So in the saying, xarajotu A^abotagiY rayoHaAna A@ll~`hi (tropical:) [ I went forth seeking, or seeking diligently, the bounty, &c., of God ]. (AO, S, TA.) And in a verse of En-Nemir Ibn-Towlab cited voce dir~apN . (S, TA.) And in the saying, in a trad., Alwaladu mino rayoHaAni A@ll~`hi (tropical:) [ Offspring are of the bounty of God ]. (S, TA.) ― -b4- It is also used (S, K) in the accus. case as an inf. n. [forming an absolute complement of a verb understood], (S,) in the sense of AisotirozaAq : so in the saying, suboHaAna A@ll~`hi wa rayoHaAnahu (assumed tropical:) [ I extol, or celebrate, or declare, the absolute perfection, or glory, or purity, of God, and beg his bounty, or his supply of the means of subsistence ]. (S, K.) ― -b5- See also rawoHN .

definition: , with damm to the r , (S, A, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: , with damm to the r , (S, A, K, &c.,) and ↓ rawoHaAniY~N , with fet-h, but this latter is deemed strange by the lexicologists [as syn. with the former], (MF,) app. rel. ns., from rawHN [in the former instance], or from rawoHN meaning the “ breath of the wind when weak ” [in the latter instance], extraordinary in form, with A and n added to the usual form of the rel. n.: (TA:) Of, or relating to, the angels and the jinn or genii: (S, A, * K:) in this sense Abu-l-Khattáb asserts himself to have heard the former used: (S:) accord. to AO, it is applied by the Arabs to anything having in it a soul, or spirit, (Sb, S,) whether a human being or a beast: (Sb:) or it has this signification also: (K:) accord. to Wardán Aboo-Khálid, as related by ISh, among the angles are those who are termed ruwHaAniy~uwna , and those who are created of light; and of the former are Jibreel and Meekáeel and Isráfeel: and ISh adds that the rwHAny~wn are souls, or spirits, which have not bodies; [ spiritual beings; ] and that the term rwHAnY~ is not applied to anything save what is of this description, such as the angles and the jinn and the like: and this is the correct explanation; not that of Ibn-El-Mudhaffar, that it signifies that into which, a soul, or spirit, has been blown. (T, TA.)

definition: , applied to a day;
sourceDefinition: , applied to a day; and raAy^iHapN , applied to a night ( layolapN ): see raAHN ; and ray~iHN . [In each case it probably has both of the meanings assigned under these two heads.] ― -b2- Also Going, or returning, [or journeying, or working, or doing a thing, (see its verb, 1,)] in the evening, or in the afternoon: (L:) [and going, or journeying, at any time of the night or day: (see, again, its verb:)] and in like manner, [but in an intensive sense,] ↓ raw^uwHN , of which the pl. is ruwHN ; and ↓ raw~aAHN , of which the pl. is raw~aAHuwna , it having no broken pl.: (L:) ↓ rawaHN is pl., (S, K,) or [rather] a quasi-pl. n., (L,) of raAy^iHN , (S, L, K,) like as xadamN is of xaAdimN . (S, L.) qawomuka raAy^iHN [ Thy people, or party, are, or is, going, &c.] is a phrase of the Arabs mentioned by Lh on the authority of Ks; but he says that it is only used thus, with a determinate noun; i. e., that one does not say qawomN raAy^iHN [though this is agreeable with analogy, as well as qawomN raAy^iHapN and qawomN raAy^iHuwna ]: one says also ↓ qawomN rawaHN and ruwHN . (L, TA.) And one says A_ibilN raAy^iHapN Camels returning in the evening, or afternoon, from pasture. (Msb.) [Hence,] maA lahu saAriHapN wa laA raAy^iHapN [lit. He has not any camels, &c., that go away to pasture, nor any that return from pasture ], meaning (assumed tropical:) he has not anything: (S:) and sometimes it means (assumed tropical:) he has not any people, or party. (Lh, TA in art. srH .) A^aEoTaAniY raAy^iHapK zawojFA occurs in a trad. as meaning He gave me, of every kind of cattle that returned to him from pasture, a portion, or sort: and in another, maAlN raAy^iHN , as meaning (assumed tropical:) [ Property, or cattle, ] of which the profit and recompense return to one: or in each, as some relate it, the word is with b [i. e. raAbiHap and raAbiH ]. (TA.) ↓ TayorN rawaHN means Birds in a state of dispersion: or returning in the evening, or afternoon, (S, K,) to their places, (S,) or to their nests: (K:) or, accord. to the T, rawaHN in this case is for rawaHapN , [a pl. of raAy^iHN ,] like kafarapN and fajarapN , [pls. of kaAfirN and faAjirN ,] and means, in this instance, in a state of dispersion. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, [used as a subst., or an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant,] A wild bull: so in the saying of El-' Ajjáj, EaAlayotu A^anosaAEiY wa juiloba Alkuwri EalaY saraApi raAy^iHK mamoTuwri i. e. [ I put my plaited thongs, and the curved pieces of wood, or the cover, of the camel's saddle, upon the back of (a camel like)] a wild bull rained upon; for when he is rained upon, he runs vehemently: (S, TA:) but the reading commonly known is, balo xilotu A^aEolaAqiY wa juiloba kuwri [ Nay, or nay rather, I fancied my bags for travelling-provisions &c. that were hung upon my camel, and the curved pieces of wood of my camel's saddle ]. (IB, TA in art. jlb . [ AElAqY is there explained as meaning “ my things that I held in high estimation: ” but the rendering that I have given I consider preferable.])

sourceDefinition: [fem. of raAy^iHN , used as a subst.,] and ↓ riyHN both signify the same; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) i. e. An accidental property or quality that is perceived by the sense of smelling; [or rather an exhalation that is so perceived; meaning odour, scent, or smell; ] (Mgh, Msb;) syn. nasiymN ; whether sweet or stinking: (K:) and the former, a sweet odour which one perceives in the nasiym [or breath of the wind ]: (L:) ↓ the latter is fem. [like the former]: (Msb:) the pl. of the former is rawaAy^iHu ; and El-Hulwánee mentions A^araAyiyHu as pl. of A^aroyaAHN [which is pl. of ↓ riyHN , under which see its other pls.]. (Mgh.) You say, Al$~aYo'i ↓ wajadotu riyHa and raAy^iHatahu in the same sense [i. e. I perceived the odour of the thing ]. (S.) And lih`*ihi Albaqolapi raAy^iHapN Tay~ibapN [ This herb, or leguminous plant, has a sweet odour ]. (L.) ― -b2- It is said in the K, that maA fiY wajohihi raAy^iHapN means (tropical:) There is not in his face any blood: but [SM says that] this requires consideration; for, accord. to A'Obeyd, one says, A^ataAnaA fulaAnN wa maA fiY wajohihi raAy^iHapu damK mino Alfaraqi (tropical:) [ Such a one came to us not having in his face any tinge of blood by reason of fright, or fear ]: and accord. to the A [and the Mgh], one says of a person who has come in fright, or fear, A^ataAnaA wa maA fiY rajohihi raAy^iHapu damK : (TA:) [accord. to Mtr, however,] one sometimes says, wa maA fiY wajohihi raAy^iHapN , without adding dm ; and an instance of this occurs in a trad. of Aboo-Jahl. (Mgh.) ― -b3- raAy^iHapN also signifies A rain of the evening or afternoon: (Lh, K:) or, as Lh says on one occasion, [simply] rain: (TA:) pl. rawaAy^iHu . (Lh, K.) ― -b4- [And] A cloud ( saHaAbapN ) that comes in the evening or afternoon. (Har p. 667.) ― -b5- See also rawaAHN .

(S, A, K.)

definition: (tropical:) Large, or liberal, in disposition;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) Large, or liberal, in disposition; (S, K, TA;) characterized by alacrity, cheerfulness, briskness, liveliness, or sprightliness, disposing him to promptness in acts of liberality, kindness, or beneficence: (S, * A, L, K: *) the former Y is said by AAF to be substituted for w : (TA. Mentioned in the L in the present art. and in art. ryH .) The Arabs have many epithets like this, [as A^ajowaliY~N and A^aHowa*iY~N and A^aHowaziY~N and A^alomaEiY~N ,] of the meansure A^afoEaliY~N , as though they were rel. ns. (TA.) ― -b2- It is also an epithet applied to a sword, meaning (assumed tropical:) That shakes, (TA, and Ham p. 358,) as though brisk, or prompt, to strike: (Ham:) or meaning of Aryah, a town of Syria, (TA and Ham, [in the latter of which the phrase suyuwfa A^aroyaHa is cited in confirmation from a poem of Sakhr el-Ghei,]) or a tribe of El-Yemen. (TA.)

definition: and ↓ zulamN An arrow without a head and without feathers: pl.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ zulamN An arrow without a head and without feathers: pl. A^azolaAmN : (S, Mgh, Msb, K:) which was applied to those [ divining- ] arrows by means of which the Arabs in the Time of Ignorance sought to know what was allotted to them: (S, K:) they were arrows upon which the Arabs in the Time of Ignorance wrote “ Command ” and “ Prohibition; ” (Mgh, Msb;) or upon some of which was written “ My Lord hath commanded me; ” and upon some, “ My Lord hath forbidden me; ” (Har p. 465;) or they were three arrows; upon one of which was written “ My Lord hath commanded me; ” and upon another, “ My Lord hath forbidden me; ” and the third was blank; (Bd in v. 4;) and they put them in a receptacle, (Mgh, Msb,) and when any one of them desired to make a journey, or to accomplish a want, (Mgh,) or when he desired to perform some affair, (Msb,) he put his hand into that receptacle, (Mgh, Msb,) and took forth an arrow; (Msb;) and if the arrow upon which was “ Command ” [or “ My Lord hath commanded me ” (Har ubi suprà)] came forth, he went to accomplish his purpose; but if that upon which was “ Prohibition ” [or “ My Lord hath forbidden me ” (Har)] came forth, he refrained; (Mgh, Msb;) and if the blank came forth, they shuffled them a second time: (Bd ubi suprà:) or, as some say, the AzlAm were white pebbles, upon which they thus wrote, and by means of which they sought to know what was allotted to them in the manner expl. above: (Har ubi suprà:) or, accord. to Az, the AzlAm [were arrows that ] belonged to Kureysh, in the Time of Ignorance, upon which were written “ He hath commanded ” and “ He hath forbidden, ” and “ Do thou ” and “ Do thou not; ” they had been well shaped ( zul~imato ) and made even, and placed in the Kaabeh, the ministers of the House taking care of them; and when a man desired to go on a journey, or to marry, he came to the minister, and said, “ Take thou forth for me a zlm ; ” and thereupon he would take it forth, and look at it; and if the arrow of command came forth, he went to accomplish that which he had purposed to do; but if the arrow of prohibition came forth, he refrained from that which he desired to do: [it is said that] there were seven of the arrows thus called with the minister of the Kaabeh, having marks upon them, and used for this purpose: (Jel in v. 4:) and sometimes there were with the man two such arrows, which he put into his sword-case; and when he desired to seek the knowledge of what was allotted to him, he took forth one of them. (TA.) Some say that the A^azolaAm are The arrows of the game called Almayosir : but this is a mistake. (TA.) The seeking to obtain the knowledge of what is allotted to one by means of the AzlAm is forbidden in the Kur v. 4. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, A^azolaAmu Albaqarapi (tropical:) The legs of the [wild] ox or cow: likened to the arrows called AzlAm because of their slenderness: or, accord. to the A, because of their strength and hardness. (TA.) [Hence, likewise,] the former of the two words ( zalamN ) signifies also (assumed tropical:) A strong and light or active boy: pl. as above: (TA:) [app. because] a poet likens [such] a boy to an arrow of the kind thus called. (S, TA. *) -A2- Also, both words, (K,) the latter on the authority of Kr, (TA,) A cloven hoof: (K:) accord. to some, peculiarly of the ox-kind: (TA:) or the [ projecting ] thing that is behind it: (S, K:) pl. as above. (K, * TA.) -A3- And the latter of the same two words, (AA, S,) or each of them, (K,) [The hyrax Syriacus; ] one of the [ animals called ] wibaAr [pl. of waborN ]: pl. as above. (AA, S, K.)

rawSourceText: and ↓ zulamN An arrow without a head and without feathers: pl. A^azolaAmN : (S, Mgh, Msb, K:) which was applied to those [ divining- ] arrows by means of which the Arabs in the Time of Ignorance sought to know what was allotted to them: (S, K:) they were arrows upon which the Arabs in the Time of Ignorance wrote “ Command ” and “ Prohibition; ” (Mgh, Msb;) or upon some of which was written “ My Lord hath commanded me; ” and upon some, “ My Lord hath forbidden me; ” (Har p. 465;) or they were three arrows; upon one of which was written “ My Lord hath commanded me; ” and upon another, “ My Lord hath forbidden me; ” and the third was blank; (Bd in v. 4;) and they put them in a receptacle, (Mgh, Msb,) and when any one of them desired to make a journey, or to accomplish a want, (Mgh,) or when he desired to perform some affair, (Msb,) he put his hand into that receptacle, (Mgh, Msb,) and took forth an arrow; (Msb;) and if the arrow upon which was “ Command ” [or “ My Lord hath commanded me ” (Har ubi suprà)] came forth, he went to accomplish his purpose; but if that upon which was “ Prohibition ” [or “ My Lord hath forbidden me ” (Har)] came forth, he refrained; (Mgh, Msb;) and if the blank came forth, they shuffled them a second time: (Bd ubi suprà:) or, as some say, the AzlAm were white pebbles, upon which they thus wrote, and by means of which they sought to know what was allotted to them in the manner expl. above: (Har ubi suprà:) or, accord. to Az, the AzlAm [were arrows that ] belonged to Kureysh, in the Time of Ignorance, upon which were written “ He hath commanded ” and “ He hath forbidden, ” and “ Do thou ” and “ Do thou not; ” they had been well shaped ( zul~imato ) and made even, and placed in the Kaabeh, the ministers of the House taking care of them; and when a man desired to go on a journey, or to marry, he came to the minister, and said, “ Take thou forth for me a zlm ; ” and thereupon he would take it forth, and look at it; and if the arrow of command came forth, he went to accomplish that which he had purposed to do; but if the arrow of prohibition came forth, he refrained from that which he desired to do: [it is said that] there were seven of the arrows thus called with the minister of the Kaabeh, having marks upon them, and used for this purpose: (Jel in v. 4:) and sometimes there were with the man two such arrows, which he put into his sword-case; and when he desired to seek the knowledge of what was allotted to him, he took forth one of them. (TA.) Some say that the A^azolaAm are The arrows of the game called Almayosir : but this is a mistake. (TA.) The seeking to obtain the knowledge of what is allotted to one by means of the AzlAm is forbidden in the Kur v. 4. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, A^azolaAmu Albaqarapi (tropical:) The legs of the [wild] ox or cow: likened to the arrows called AzlAm because of their slenderness: or, accord. to the A, because of their strength and hardness. (TA.) [Hence, likewise,] the former of the two words ( zalamN ) signifies also (assumed tropical:) A strong and light or active boy: pl. as above: (TA:) [app. because] a poet likens [such] a boy to an arrow of the kind thus called. (S, TA. *) -A2- Also, both words, (K,) the latter on the authority of Kr, (TA,) A cloven hoof: (K:) accord. to some, peculiarly of the ox-kind: (TA:) or the [ projecting ] thing that is behind it: (S, K:) pl. as above. (K, * TA.) -A3- And the latter of the same two words, (AA, S,) or each of them, (K,) [The hyrax Syriacus; ] one of the [ animals called ] wibaAr [pl. of waborN ]: pl. as above. (AA, S, K.)

definition: Suffering from indigestion, or heaviness of the stomach arising from food which it is too weak to digest: (JK, K:) and zhmAn with damm [i.
sourceDefinition: Suffering from indigestion, or heaviness of the stomach arising from food which it is too weak to digest: (JK, K:) and zhmAn with damm [i. e. ↓ zuhomaAnN , with tenween, for, as is said in the S (voce EuroyaAnN ), a word of the measure fuEolaAn has its fem. with p meaning, if an epithet,] signifies [the same, or] satiated, sated, or satisfied in stomach; as also ↓ zuhomaAniY~N . (Z, cited by Freytag in his Arab. Prov., ii. 196.) And [hence, app.,] zahomaAnu , (Abu-n-Nedà, IAar, TA,) or ↓ zuhomaAnu , [imperfectly decl. (like the first word) as a proper name ending with An ] (AHeyth, IDrd, S, TA,) or each, (K,) the name of A certain dog. (S, K, &c.) It is said in a prov., zaAduhu ↓ fiY baToni zahomaAna In the belly of the dog zhmAn is his provision: applied to a man who has with him his apparatus, and what he needs: or, accord. to AA, the case was this: a man slaughtered a camel, and divided it, and gave to [one whose name was] zhmAn his share, and then zhmAn returned to receive again with the [other] people; and it is applied to a man who seeks a thing when he has received once: (Meyd:) Z says that zahomaAnu is the name of a man who came to a people that had slaughtered a camel, and asked them to give him some food thereof, and they gave it him: then he returned to them, and they said to him thus, meaning “ Thou has had thy provision thereof, and it is in thy belly; ” and it is applied to any one who has received his share of a thing, and then come, after that, seeking it: or, as some relate it, it is with damm, [↓ zuhomaAn ] and is applied to one who is invited to a repast when he is satiated: or it relates to one suffering from indigestion: or zhmAn is the name of a dog; and it originated from the fact that a man prepared for himself some provision, and was unmindful of it, and a dog ate it; and it is applied to him for whom there is no share. (Z cited by Freytag ubi suprà.)

definition: The odour of fat and stinking flesh-meat;
sourceDefinition: The odour of fat and stinking flesh-meat; (JK, K; [and mentioned also, but not explained, in the S;]) as also ↓ zuhomapN : (K:) or the latter signifies a fetid odour [in a general sense]: (S:) but accord. to Az, the former signifies the disagreeableness of odour, without the being fetid, or altered [ for the worse ]; such as the odour of lean flesh-meat, or the odour of the flesh of a beast of prey, or strong-smelling sea-fish; the fish of the rivers having no zhwmp . (TA.) [See also 1, first sentence; and ruhomN , last signification; and zahamN .]

definition: , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor. yaziydu , (S, Mgh, Msb,) inf. n. ziyaAdapN (S, A, * Msb, K *) and zayodN , (S, Mgh, Msb, K, *) with which are syn. ziydN (S, K) and zayadN (K) and maziydN (S, K) and zayodaAnN , which last is anomalous, like $anoA=nN (K) and lay~aAnN , said to be the only instances of the kind, (TA,) all as inf. ns., (TK,) and so is mazaAdN , (TA,) and J adds that zuwaAdapN is mentioned by Yaakoob, from Ks, from El-Bekree, as syn. with ziyaAdapN , but this is a mistake, which is unfairly imputed to J by the author of the K, (MF,) [who says,] as to Alz~uwaAdapu , it is a mistranscription by J, for the words are Alz~uwaArapu and Alz~iyaArapu , [in the CK Alr~uwAdpu and Alr~iyAdpu ,] with r , and without the mention of [the signification of] Aln~umuw~u , (K, TA,) It (a thing, S, Mgh, Msb, [as, for ex.,] water, and property, A) increased, or augmented, or grew; (S, A, TA;) [and in like manner said of a man, and of any animal;] as also ↓ AizodaAda : (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K:) or this latter has a more intensive signification than the former, like Aikotasaba in relation to kasaba . (MF. [See also 5.]) In this sense it has a single objective complement; as in zaAda ka*aA It, or he, increased, or augmented, or grew, in such a thing; as also ↓ AizodaAda . (TA.) [The latter is more commonly used in this manner.] You say, ↓ Aizodadotu maAlFA (A, Mgh, Msb) [ I increased in property: also] meaning I increased to myself, or for myself, property. (Mgh, * Msb.) And AlA^amoru ↓ AzdAd SuEuwbapF [ The affair increased in difficulty ]. (A.) ― -b2- [Also It exceeded; it was, or became, redundant, or superfluous; it remained over and above. And zaAda Ealayohi It exceeded it; as also ↓ tzAyd .] You say, zaAda EalaY Al$~aYo'i DiEofahu [ It exceeded the thing by the like thereof, or more ]. (A.) And zaAda EalaY maA A^araAda [ It exceeded what he desired ]. (A.) ― -b3- Also He gave an addition: so in the saying, faqado A^arobaY ↓ mano zaAda waA@zodaAda He who gives an addition, and who takes it, [each of these] practises usury. (Msb.) ― -b4- [And He added, or exaggerated. ] yaziydu fiY Hadiyvihi [ He adds, or exaggerates, in his narration, or talk, or discourse, ] is said of a liar. (A and TA voce sar~aAjN . [See also 5.]) -A2- It is also trans.: (Msb:) you say, zaAdahu , aor. yaziyduhu , inf. n. ziyaAdapN , He increased it, or augmented it. (L.) And in this sense it is doubly trans.: (MF:) you say, zaAdahu A@ll~`hu xayorFA , (S, K,) or maAlFA , (A,) [ God increased to him, or added to him, good fortune or prosperity or the like, or property; increased, or added to, his good fortune, &c.; or may God increase &c.;] as also ↓ zay~adahu : (K:) and zaAda fiymaA Einodahu , (S,) or fiY maAlihi , (A,) [ He increased, or added to, what he possessed or his possessions, or his property; or may He (i. e. God) increase &c.] ― -b2- zaAdahu also signifies He gave him an increase, or an addition, or more. (Msb.) See 10. ― -b3- You say also, maA yaziyduka A^aHadN Ealayohi [ No one is more sufficient for thee than he ]. (K in art. znd . [See 4 in that art.]) And laA yaziyduka Ealayohi jamalN No camel will be more sufficient for thee than he; i. q. laA yaDur~uka . (ISk, S in art. Dr [in which see other exs.].)

definition: It (a price, S, A) was, or became, excessive, or dear;
sourceDefinition: It (a price, S, A) was, or became, excessive, or dear; (S, A, K;) as also ↓ tzAyd . (A, TA.) ― -b2- He added, or exaggerated, (MA,) or lied, (S, MA, K,) in narration, or discourse. (S, MA. [See also 1, latter half.]) And He affected to exceed the due bounds in his narration, or discourse, and his speech; (TA;) he affected excess in speech, &c.; (K, TA;) i. e. in speech and in action; (TA;) as also ↓ tzAyd : (K:) or Alt~azay~udu fiY AlHadiyvi means the embellishing narration, or discourse, with lies, and adding in it what does not belong to it. (Har p. 195.) In the verse of 'Adee cited in art. znd , the last word is tazay~adi as some relate it, or tazan~adi as others relate it. (TA.) ― -b3- He went a pace exceeding that termed AlEanaq . (S, K. [See also *amala , and naSaba Als~ayora , and wasaja .]) And tzy~dt She (A camel) stretched forth her neck, and went a pace exceeding that termed AlEanaq , as though she were swimming with her rider: (A, TA:) and in like manner one says of a mare, or horse. (TA.) And tzy~dt AlA_ibilu fiY sayorihaA The camels tasked themselves in their pace beyond their ability. (TA.)

AstzAd He sought, or desired, or demanded, an increase, an addition, or more; (A, Mgh, Msb;) as also ↓ AizodaAda ; whence the saying, to a man to whom a thing has been given, ↓ halo tazodaAdu Dost thou seek, or desire, or demand, more than what I have given thee? sourceDefinition: an inf. n. of zaAda . (S, Msb.) Using it as an inf. n., (Msb,) you say, AifoEalo *`lika ziyaAdapF [meaning Do thou that in addition ]: (S, Msb:) the vulgar say ↓ zaAy^idapF , (S,) which one should not say. (Msb.) [Hence also,] Huruwfu Alz~iyaAdapi [ The letters of augmentation; or the augmentative letters; i. e. the letters that are added to the radical letters in Arabic words ]: they are ten, and are comprised in the saying, saA^alotumuwniyhaA [“ Ye asked me for them ”], (TA,) and in A^aloyawoma tanosaAhu [“ Today thou wilt forget it ”]; (K, TA;) and more than a hundred and thirty other combinations comprising them have been mentioned: (MF:) [these letters are also called zawaAy^idu , of which the sing. is ↓ zaAy^idapN .] See also zayodN . ― -b2- [As a simple subst., or a subst. properly so termed, it signifies An increase, or increment; and augmentation, or augment; an addition, additament, adjunct, or accessory: an accession: excess, redundance, or superfluity: and a redundant part or portion or appertenance; a surplus; a residue: an excrescence: pl. ziyaAdaAtN and zayAy^idu . ― -b3- Hence,] A_ibilN kaviyrapu Alz~ayaAy^idi i.e. Alz~iyaAdaAt [ Camels having much increase; lit., much, or many, increases ]. (K.) A poet says, bihajomapK tamolaA^u Eayona AlHaAsidi *aAti suruwHK jam~api Alz~ayaAy^idi [ With a herd of forty or more camels, that fill, or glut, the eye of the envier, enjoying pasturing by themselves, having much increase ]: some say, [in citing this verse,] Alz~awaAy^idi , which is pl. of ↓ zaAy^idapN ; but AlzwAy^d is said only in relation to the legs of a beast. (L.) ― -b4- [Hence also,] ziyaAdapu Alkabidi , (so in a copy of the S, and in the A and L, and in several places in the K,) or Alkabidi ↓ zaAy^idapu , (so termed by Zj, and so in the T, and in two copies of the S, and in the L,) both of which are correct, (TA,) [ The redundant appertenance of the liver; ] a certain small piece to which the liver is attached, or suspended: (Zj, in his “ Khalk el-Insán: ”) or a certain small appertenance of the liver ( hunay~apN minohaA SagiyrapN ), at its side, going away from it ( mutanaH~iyapN EanohaA ): (S, L:) or a certain piece appended, or attached, to the liver ( muEal~aqapN bihaA ): (A:) or a certain appendage of the liver; [so I render hanapN mutaEal~iqapN minohaA , agreeably with the next preceding explanation; though it may be rendered a thing suspended from it, i.e. from the liver; or the right reading may be hnp mtEl~qp bihaA , which is virtually the same as the explanation in the A, and agreeable with what here follows: so called] because it is a redundance ( taziydu ) upon its upper surface: (L:) [all of these explanations seem to denote the round ligament of the liver: the Hebrew יֹחֶרֶח הַכּבֵד , in Ex. xxix. 22, literally signifies the same; like the slightly-varying appellations in Ex. xxix. 13 and Lev. iii. 4, and Lev. ix. 10: but the real meaning thereof is much disputed: the rendering of the LXX. is λοβὸσ τοῦ ἥπατοσ ; which is said to mean extrema pars hepatis: that of the Vulg., reticulum hepatis: that of our authorized Engl. Vers., the caul above the liver; (with this marginal note: “ it seemeth by anatomy, and the Hebrew Doctors, to be the midriff: ” ) and it is remarkable that this is one of the meanings assigned to Alxilobu , which some hold to be syn. with zayaAdapu Alkabidi : (see xilobN :) Bochart (in his Hieroz. t. i., p. 498, seq.,) and Gesenius (in his Lex.) explain the Hebrew term as meaning the greater lobe of the liver: but this is hard to reconcile with the Hebrew or the Arabic; and utterly irreconcileable with the explanations given by the Arabs; among whom, it should be observed, were many of the Jewish religion, who cannot reasonably be supposed to have not known the correct meaning of a term relating to their sacrifices:] the pl. of zyAdp is zayaAy^idu , (L,) and that of ↓ zAy^dp is zawaAy^idu . (S, L.) Hence the saying, Alwaladu kabidu *iY Alwaladi wawaladu Alwaladi ziyaAdapu Alkabidi [ The child is as the liver of the parent, and the grandchild is as the redundant appertenance of the liver ]. (A, TA.)

sourceDefinition: [ A leathern water-bag, one of a pair which is borne by a camel or other beast; ] the half ( $aTor ) of a raAwiyap : (Msb in art. zwd :) [a water-bag of this kind is represented in a sketch of “ Sakkàs ” in my work on the Modern Egyptians:] it has two loops, and two kidney-shaped pieces of leather ( kuloyataAni ), the former of which are sewed to the latter: (TA voce xurobapN :) the raAwiyap consists of two mezádehs ( mazaAdataAni ), which are bound upon the two sides of the camel with the [ cord called ] riwaA=' : the pl. is mazaAyidu [often written mazaAy^idu ]; and sometimes the Arabs elided the p , saying ↓ mazaAdN : (T, TA:) [both of these forms are mentioned in the S and K as pls.:] and ↓ mazaAdN without p , is [also] applied to the single one ( farodap [meaning the single water-skin ]) which the rider attaches behind his camel's saddle, having no EazolaA=' , [or spout (which is closed by means of a thong tied round it) at one of the lower extremities for pouring out the water; thus] differing from the mazaAdap : (T, TA:) or the mzAdp is a raAwiyap , [app. accord. to some who applied this latter term to a single water-bag,] (S, A, K,) or only (K) such as is composed of two skins with a third inserted between them to widen it: (A 'Obeyd, S, M, A, K:) and so are the saTiyHap and the $aEiyb : (A 'Obeyd, S:) or the saTyHp is made of two skins put face to face; and the mzAdp is of two skins and a half, or of three skins: (ISh, TA:) or it is [ a water-bag ] joined ( ma$oEurbap ) at one side; if consisting of two faces ( An xrjt mn wjhyn [i. e. of two pieces of skin whereof each forms one face or side]) it is called a $aEiyb : or it is like a rAwyp having no EazolaA=' [expl. above]: AM and the author of the Msb and some others assert that its medial radical letter is w , and that it is from Alz~awodu , (TA,) being so called because one furnishes himself with water in it for travellingprovision: (Msb in art. zwd :) but this is a mistake: (TA:) it is thus called because it is enlarged by the addition of a third skin: (AO, El-Khafájee, TA:) [Fei says that] accord. to analogy it should be mizaAdapN . (Msb in art. zwd .)

sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. sajorN (Msb, TA) and sujuwrN ; (TA;) and ↓ sj~rhu , inf. tasojiyrN ; (TA;) He filled it; (S, A, Msb, K;) namely, a river, or channel for water; (S, A, K;) and a vessel; as also sakarahu ; (TA;) with water. (S.) You say, sajara Als~ayolu AlA=baAra [ The torrent filled the wells ]. (A.) And sujirati Alv~imaAdu The vmAd [see its sing. vamadN ] became filled by the rain. (S.) In the Kur [lxxxi. 6], wa A_i*aA A@lobiHaAru sujirato , some read thus; and others, ↓ suj~irato ; (Zj;) and Th explains it, and so Zj the former reading, as signifying, And when the seas shall be filled: but ISd says that there is no way of understanding this unless it mean filled with fire: or it means and when the seas shall overflow: or shall meet together and become one sea: (TA:) or ↓ suj~irato signifies shall flow forth, one into another, and thus become one sea, (Zj, Bd,) and so be filled: (Bd:) and there are other explanations of the above-mentioned words of the Kur, which see below. ― -b2- sajara AlmaA='a fiY Haloqihi He poured the water into his throat. (K.) ― -b3- sajara Alt~an~uwra , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. , inf. n. sajorN ; (S;) and ↓ sj~rhu ; (Bd in lxxxi. 6;) or the latter has an intensive signification; (Mgh;) He heated the oven; (S, A, K;) kindled fire in it: (Msb:) or filled it with firewood, to heat it: (Mgh Bd:) or he heated it fully with fuel. (TA.) The words of the Kur quoted above, w A*A AlbHAr sujirato , are said to signify And when the seas shall be set on fire: (El-Hasan El-Basree:) or shall become without water, (Katádeh,) or shall be dried up, by the kindling of fire therein: (B:) or shall be kindled, and become fire: (Jel:) or shall be mixed together, and dry up, and become fire; (El-Ubbee;) an explanation founded upon the license to employ a homonym in its several significations together: (MF:) or by “ sea ” is meant hell. (Kaab.) You say also, sajara Alwaquwda biA@lomisojarapi [ He stirred the fuel with the msjrp ]. (A.) -A2- sajarati Aln~aAqapu , (S, A, K,) aor. , (S,) inf. n. sajorN (S, A, K) and sujuwrN ; (S, K;) and ↓ sj~rt , inf. n. tasojiyrN ; (A;) (tropical:) The she-camel prolonged her yearning cry ( Haniyn , S, A, K) after her young one, (As, A,) and filled her mouth with it. (A.) -A3- sajarahu , inf. n. sajorN ; [and ↓ sj~rhu , and ↓ sawojarahu ; (see the pass. part. ns., below;)] He made it [namely hair or the like] to hang down. (TA. [See also sarajato $aEorahaA .]) -A4- sajarahu ; (A, K;) and ↓ sj~rhu , (A,) inf. n. tasojiyrN ; (TA;) and ↓ sawojarahu ; (IJ, A, K;) He put a saAjuwr upon, or around, his (a dog's) neck: (A:) or he bound him (a dog) with a sAjwr . (K.)

definition: , (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, M, Msb, K,) inf. n. sad~N ; (S, M, Mgh, Msb;) and ↓ sd~d ; (M;) [but the latter has an intensive signification, or relates to several objects;] He closed, or closed up, an interstice, or intervening space: (M:) and stopped, or stopped up, (M,) or repaired, and made firm or strong, (S, A, K,) a breach, or gap, (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) and the like. (S, Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence one says,] sud~ato Ealayohi AlT~ariyqu (assumed tropical:) [ The road, or way, became closed, or stopped, against him ]. (K.) And sud~a Tariyquhu mino bayoni yadayohi wamano xalofihi (assumed tropical:) [ His road, or way, became closed, or stopped, before him and behind him ]. (Zj, M.) And sad~a AlA^ufuqa (tropical:) [ It obstructed the horizon ]; said of a multitudinous swarm of locusts. (S, A, * K.) And sad~a Ealayohimo , and ↓ A^asad~a , It closed, or obstructed, against them, the horizon; [ AlA^ufuqa being understood;] said of a collection of clouds rising. (M.) And sad~a maA waraA='ahu [ It barred, or excluded, what was behind it ]. (M.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] sadadotu Ealayohi baAba AlkalaAmi (assumed tropical:) [ I closed, or stopped, to him the door of speech; i. e.] I prevented him from speaking; as though I closed, or stopped, his mouth. (Msb.) And maA sadadotu EalaY lahawaAti xaSomK qaT~u (assumed tropical:) I never stopped the way of speech of an adversary, nor prevented his saying what was in his mind. (Shureyh, Mgh.) And maA sadadotu EalaY xaSomK qaT~u (assumed tropical:) I never stopped an adversary from speaking; (El-Fáïk, Mgh, L;) on the authority of Esh-Shaabee: (Mgh:) occurring in a trad. (L.) ― -b4- And A^abiyhi ↓ huwa yasud~u masad~a (tropical:) [ He fills up, or supplies, the place of his father ]: and A^asolaAfihimo ↓ yasud~uwna masad~a (tropical:) [ They fill up, or supply, the place of their ancestors ]. (A, TA.) And yusad~u bihi AlHaAjapu (tropical:) Want is supplied thereby: (M, * TA:) [whence the saying,] taSad~aquwA walawo bitamorapK faA_in~ahaA tasud~u mina AljaAy^iEi (assumed tropical:) [ Give ye something as alms, though it be but a date, or a dried date; for it will supply somewhat of the want of the hungry ]: a trad. (El-Jámi' es-Sagheer.) And yasud~u Alr~amaqa (assumed tropical:) [ It stays, or arrests, the remains of life; as though it stopped the passage of the last breath from the body; or] it maintains, and preserves, the strength. (Msb in art. rmq .) ― -b5- And sad~ahu (assumed tropical:) He attributed, or imputed, to him, or he charged him with, or accused him of, a fault; [as though he thereby stopped his mouth; (see sad~N ;)] as also sat~ahu . (TA in art. st .) -A2- sad~a , aor. yasid~u , (S, L, K,) with kesr, (S,) inf. n. sadaAdN and suduwdN , (L, the former inf. n. expl. in the S and K as signifying AisotiqaAmapN ,) said of a spear, and an arrow, (TA,) and a saying, (S,) and an action, (TA,) or a thing [absolutely]; (L;) or sad~a , [sec. pers. sadidota ,] aor. yasad~u , with fet-h to the s , (A,) inf. n. sadadN , (TK, expl. in the S and K as signifying AisotiqaAmapN , like sadaAdN , of which it is said in the S to be a contraction,) said of a saying, and an affair; (A;) or sad~a , aor. yasid~u and yasad~u , inf. n. sadadN ; (MA;) i. q. SaAra sadiydFA [i. e. It was, or became, right, direct, or in a right state; it had, or took, a right direction or tendency; it tended towards the right point or object ]: (S, A, L, K, TA:) and [in like manner] ↓ Astd~ is syn. with AisotaqaAma [which signifies the same]; (S, K;) as also ↓ Asd~ and ↓ tsd~d : (TA:) ↓ Astd~ said of an affair signifies it was, or became, rightly ordered or disposed; in a right state. (Msb.) You say, lahu ↓ tsd~d and ↓ Astd~ It was, or became, rightly directed towards it. (M.) And saAEiduhu ↓ Astd~ and ↓ tsd~d His fore arm was, or became, in a right state, or rightly directed, EalaY Alr~amoYi [ for shooting ]; syn. AstqAm . (A.) A poet says, saAEiduhu ramaAniY ↓ falam~aA A@sotad~a A^uEal~imuhu Alr~imaAyapa kul~a yawomK [ I teaching him the art of shooting every day; and when his fore arm became in a right state, he shot me ]: As says that [the reading] A$td~ , with $ , is not to be regarded. (S, TA.) ― -b2- And sad~a , aor. yasid~u , with kesr to the s , (A, Msb, TA,) inf. n. suduwdN (Msb) [and app. also, as above, sadaAdN , q. v. infrà], is said of a man, (A, Msb, TA,) in like manner meaning SaAra sadiydFA [i. e. He was, or became, in a right state; he had, or took, a right direction or tendency; he tended towards the right point or object ]: (A, TA:) or, (Msb,) as also ↓ Asd~ , (S, K, TA,) he hit the right thing (S, Msb, K, TA,) in his saying (S, Msb, TA) and in his action: (Msb:) or ↓ Asd~ signifies he said, or did, what was right: (Msb:) or he sought what was right; (L, K;) as also ↓ sd~d ; (L;) or it has this last meaning also. (S, * L.) You say, fiY Alqawoli ↓ A_in~ahu layusid~u Verily he hits the right thing in the saying. (S, L.) And qado maA $iy^ota ↓ A^asodadota (S, * L) is said to a man when he seeks [or has sought] what is right, (S,) meaning Thou hast sought what is right; whether the person thus addressed have hit the right thing or not. (L.) One says also, sad~a Ealayoka Alr~ajulu , aor. yasid~u , inf. n. sd [app. a mistranscription for sadaAd or suduwd ], The man said, or did, what was right [ against thee ]: so in the handwriting of Sh. (Az, TA.)

sourceDefinition: and ↓ sud~N Any building, or construction, with which a place is closed or closed up, or stopped or stopped up: (M: [see also sidaAdN :]) a dam: (Msb:) a thing intervening, as a separation, a partition, a fence, a barrier, a rampart, or an obstacle, or obstruction, between two other things; (S, Msb, K:) and a mountain: (S, M, K: [in the last it seems that this meaning is restricted to the former word; but if restricted to either, it should be to the latter:]) or, as some say, anything that faces one, or is over against one, and bars, or excludes, ( yasud~u ,) what is behind it: whence goats are said to be sad~N yuraY mino waraAy^ihi Alfaqoru (assumed tropical:) [ a barrier behind which is seen poverty ]; meaning that they are not of great utility: (M:) or sad~N signifies what is made by man; and sud~N , what is created by God, (Zj, M, Msb, K,) as a mountain: (Msb:) in the Kur xviii. 92 and 93, and xxxvi. 8, some read with fet-h, and some with damm: (M, TA:) the pl. is A^asodaAdN , [a pl. of pauc.,] (A, Msb,) or A^asid~apN , [also a pl. of pauc.,] and suduwdN , [a pl. of mult.,] the latter of these two agreeable with general analogy, and the former of them anomalous, or, [ISd says,] in my opinion, this ( A^asid~apN ) is pl. of sidaAdN . (M.) You say, Duriba bayonahumaA sad~N and sud~N [ A barrier, or an obstacle, was set between them two ]: and Duribato bayonahumaA AlA^asodaAdu [ Barriers, or obstacles, were set between them two ]. (A.) And Darabato Ealayohi AlA^aroDu biAlA^asodaAdi (tropical:) [ The earth, or land, set barriers, or obstacles, against him ]; meaning, the ways became closed, or stopped, against him, and the courses that he should pursue became obscure to him: (K: in the CK Duribato :) the sing. of A^asodaAdN [accord. to general analogy] is sud~N . (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] the former ( sad~N ) also signifies, (Fr, S, M, L, K,) or ↓ sidaAdN , (A,) or the former and ↓ sadaAdapN , (L,) (tropical:) A fault, or defect, (Fr, S, M, A, &c.,) such as blindness and deafness and dumbness, (S,) or such as closes, or stops, one's mouth, so that he does not speak: (A:) pl. of the first, (S, M, K,) or of the second, (A,) A^asid~apN , [a pl. of pauc.,] (S, M, A, K,) accord. to analogy suduwdN , (S, M, K,) or A^asud~N [which is a pl. of pauc.]. (M.) You say, ↓ maA bihi sidaAdN (tropical:) There is not in him any fault &c.: and fulaAnN bariYo'N mina AlA^asid~api (tropical:) Such a one is free from faults &c. (A.) And tasud~u faAhu Eani AlkalaAmi ↓ maA bifulaAnK sadaAdapN (assumed tropical:) There is not in such a one a fault that stops his mouth from speaking. (Aboo-Sa'eed, L.) And laA tajoEalan~a bijanobika AlA^asid~apa (tropical:) By no means render thou thy bosom contracted so that thou shalt be unable to return an answer, like him who is deaf or dumb. (S, K.) ― -b3- See also sud~N . ― -b4- sd~ [so in the TA, i. e. either sad~N or sud~a ,] also signifies (assumed tropical:) A she-camel by which the sportsman conceals himself from the game; also called dariyoy^apNnd dariyEapN whence the saying, ramaAhu fiY sd~i naAqatihi (assumed tropical:) [ He shot him, or shot at him, by his she-camel whereby he was concealing himself ]. (IAar, TA.) ― -b5- And sad~N , (M,) or sud~N , (O, K,) is also syn. with Zil~N [as meaning (tropical:) Shade, or shadow; or cover, or protection ]. (IAar, M, O, K, TA.) A poet cited by IAar says, qaEadotu lahu fiY sad~i niqoDK muEaw~adK li*`lika fiY SaHoraA='a ji*omK dariynuhaA (tropical:) [ I sat for him, i. e. lay in wait for him, in the shade, or cover, of a camel rendered lean by travel, accustomed to that, in a desert whereof the dry herbage was old ]: i. e. I made him a cover, or screen, to me, in order that he might not see me: and by ji*om he means “ old, ” because Alji*omu signifies AlA^aSolu , and there is nothing older than the A^aSol ; and he uses it as an epithet because it implies the meaning of an epithet. (M.) -A2- sad~N also signifies A thing, (S, K,) [i. e.] a [ basket such as is called ] sal~ap , (M, TA,) made of twigs, (S, M, K,) and having covers ( A^aTobaAq ): (S, K: [but this addition in the S and K seems properly to apply to the pl., as will be shown by what follows:]) pl. sidaAdN and suduwdN : (M, TA:) or, accord. to Lth, suduwdN signifies [ baskets such as are called ] silaAl , [pl. of sal~apN ,] made of twigs, and having covers ( A^aTobaAq ); one of which is called [not sad~N but] ↓ sad~apN : and it is said also on other authority that the sal~ap is called sad~apN and TabolN . (L, TA.)

(A.) ― -b2- Hence, Umm-Selemeh, addressing' Áïsheh, termed her a sud~ap , i. e. a baAb [meaning (assumed tropical:) A means of communication [, between the Prophet and his people. sourceDefinition: [an inf. n. of the intrans. verb sad~a ; as also ↓ sadadN ]. [Hence,] one says, A_in~ahu la*uw sadaAdK Verily he has a faculty of hitting the right thing, or his object or aim, in speaking, and in the managing or disposing of affairs, and in shooting. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence also, as a subst.,] A thing that is right, syn. SawaAbN , (S, A, Msb, K,) and qaSodN , (S,) of what is said and of what is done; (S, A, * Msb, K;) as also ↓ sadadN , (S, A,) which is a contraction of the former. (S.) One says, qaAla sadaAdFA mina Alqawoli He said a right thing [lit. of what is said, i. e., a right saying ]; (S, A;) as also ↓ sadadFA . (A.) And yuSiybu Als~adaAda He hits the right thing in speech [or action]. (S.) And huwa EalaY sadaAdK mino A^amorihi and ↓ sadadK [ He is following a right course of action in respect of his affair ]. (A.) And A^amoru fulaAnK yajoriY EalaY Als~adaAdi The affair of such a one goes on according to that which is right. (S.) ― -b3- [And hence the saying,] A^atatonaA riyHN mino sadaAdi A^aroDihimo (tropical:) A wind came to us from the direction of their land. (A, TA.) ― -b4- It is also used as an epithet, syn. with sadiydN , q. v. (L.) ― -b5- And Als~adaAdu [as though meaning The right projecter ] is a name that was given to a bow belonging to the Prophet, as ominating the hitting of the object aimed at by that which was shot from it. (TA.) -A2- See also sidaAdN , in three places.

definition: A thing with which an interstice, or intervening space, is closed, or closed up: (AO, M, L: [see also sad~N :]) and a thing with which a breach, or gap, (M, A,) is stopped, or stopped up, (M,) or repaired, and made firm or strong: (A:) pl.
sourceDefinition: A thing with which an interstice, or intervening space, is closed, or closed up: (AO, M, L: [see also sad~N :]) and a thing with which a breach, or gap, (M, A,) is stopped, or stopped up, (M,) or repaired, and made firm or strong: (A:) pl. A^asid~apN . (M.) Primarily, accord. to ISh, (Meyd, in explanation of a prov. mentioned in what follows,) Somewhat of milk that dries up in the orifice of a she-camel's teat; (Meyd, K;) because it stops up the passage of the milk. (Meyd.) Also A stopper of a bottle (S, * Mgh, * Msb, K, * TA) &c.: (Msb:) in this sense [as well as in those before mentioned] with kesr (S, Mgh, Msb, K) only [to the s ]: and so in the sense next following. (S, K.) A body of horse and foot serving as blockaders of the frontier of a hostile country. (S, K, * TA.) ― -b2- sidaAdN mino EawazK and ↓ sadaAdN , (ISk, S, M, Msb, K,) but the former is the more chaste, (S,) and it alone is mentioned by most authors in this saying, because it is from sdAd as meaning the “ stopper ” of a bottle; (Msb;) and some say that ↓ sadAd , with fet-h, is a corruption; (Msb, K;) expressly disallowed by As and ISh; (Msb;) a prov.; (Meyd;) meaning (tropical:) A thing by which want is supplied, (S, M, Msb, K,) and by which life is preserved; accord. to ISh, if incomplete; and accord. to As, a thing by which somewhat of the entire wants of one's case is supplied. (Msb.) One says also, A^aSabotu bihi sidaAdFA mina AlEayo$i and ↓ sadaAdFA (tropical:) I attained thereby a thing by which want was supplied; (S, K, * TA;) or a means of sustaining life. (AO, L.) ― -b3- See also sad~N , in two places.

sourceDefinition: : see 1, first sentence. ― -b2- [Hence,] A^asofafotu Al$~aYo'a , inf. n. A_isofaAfN , I stuck one part of the thing to another. (Yz, TA.) ― -b3- [And from the same signification, as is indicated in the O and TA,] As~f Aln~aZara (tropical:) He looked sharply, (S, M, A, O, K,) and hardly, (S, O,) and minutely, (A,) towards, or at, ( A_ilaY ,) a person, (S, A, O,) and an affair, (A,) and AAF adds, and inclined towards the ground. (M.) -A2- Also He fed a camel with dry herbage. (K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Asf~ Alfarasa AllijaAma (assumed tropical:) He put the bit into the mouth of the horse. (Moheet, L, K.) ― -b3- And Asf~ Ald~awaA='a (assumed tropical:) He stuffed the wound with the medicament: (M:) or Asf~ AljuroHa dawaA='F (tropical:) he put a medicament into the wound; (K, TA;) as though he put safuwf to it. (TA.) ― -b4- And Asf~ Alwa$oma naw^uwrFA (assumed tropical:) He filled in the tattoo with nw^wr [i. e. smoke-black of fat ]. (M.) ― -b5- And A^usif~a wajohuhu Aln~aw^uwra (assumed tropical:) His face was sprinkled with nw^wr . (S.) It is said in a trad., fakaA^an~amaA A^usif~a wajohuhu , meaning (assumed tropical:) His face was altered, (S, K, *) as though something that altered it had been sprinkled upon it. (S.) You say also, kaA^an~a wajohahu A^usif~a ramaAdFA , meaning (assumed tropical:) His face became of a blackish, or an ashy, hue, altered, as though ashes had been sprinkled upon it: and ↓ suf~a Alr~amaAdu fiY wajohihi (assumed tropical:) [ Ashes were sprinkled upon his face ], meaning his face became altered. (Har p. 626.) -A3- Also It approached the earth, or ground; (S, M, K;) said of a bird in its flight; (S, K;) or of a bird &c.: (M:) or it (a bird) flew over the ground so near that its feet almost reached it. (A.) And Asf~t Als~aHaAbapu The cloud approached the earth. (S, K.) ― -b2- Said of a stallion, He stooped his head to bite. (M, K.) And one says of man, Asf~ mina AlA^aroDi [and A_ilaY AlArD He stooped towards the ground ]. (O in art. $b .) ― -b3- And, said of a man, (S,) (assumed tropical:) He pursued small, or little, things: (S, K:) and (assumed tropical:) he followed after low, or mean, things: (K:) [(assumed tropical:) he stooped to such things: ] or Asf~ A_ilaY madaAqi AlA^umuwri wa A^alaAy^imihaA (assumed tropical:) He approached [or pursued ] small, or little, things, and the meanest, or most ignoble, thereof; or became mean, or ignoble: (M, * TA:) and Asf~ liloA^amori Ald~aniY~ , [or correctly Ald~aniYo'i ,] and A_ilayohi , (assumed tropical:) He approached [ the thing that was near, or that was low, or mean ]; from Asf~ said of a bird in its flight, meaning It approached the ground so that its feet almost touched it. (Har p. 206.) [Hence the saying,] taHaf~aZo mino Algamali Als~afosaAfi walaAtusif~a lahu baEoDa lA_isofaAfi (tropical:) [ Guard thyself from the bad action, and approach it not with any degree of approaching ]. (TA.) ― -b4- You say also, maAA^asaf~a minohu bitaAfihK He obtained not [ from him, or of it, a paltry acquisition ], (K, TA,) [or] anything. (TA.) ― -b5- And Asf~ He fled from his companion, (K, TA,) running most vehemently. (TA.)

definition: The dust of flour, that rises, (K,) or flies and rises, (TA,) at the sifting.
sourceDefinition: The dust of flour, that rises, (K,) or flies and rises, (TA,) at the sifting. (K, TA.) ― -b2- The fine particles or dust: (S, Mgh, K:) or such as rises, or spreads, of dust. (M.) ― -b3- Hence, (Mgh,) safosaAfu Al$iEori (Mgh, K) (assumed tropical:) What is bad of poetry, (K, TA,) imperfectly, or unsoundly, done. (TA. [In the CK, Al$~aEari is erroneously put for Al$iEori ; and Freytag appears to have read Al$~aEiyri .]) safosaAfN signifies (assumed tropical:) Bad poetry: and (assumed tropical:) anything imperfectly, or unsoundly, done. (M.) Anything bad. (S, K. [Compare the Hebr. אֲסַפְסֻף occurring with the article, and with the quiescent, in Numbers xi. 4.]) (assumed tropical:) Such as is bad of natural dispositions. (M.) And (assumed tropical:) A contemptible, or despicable, thing or affair. (S, K.) It is said in a trad., A_in~a A@ll~`ha yuHib~u maEaAliYa AlA^amuwri wa yubogiDu safosaAfahaA , (S, M, Mgh, TA,) or yakorahu safosaAfahaA , (S, TA,) i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ Verily God loves lofty things, or things whereby one acquires eminence or nobility, and ] hates paltry, and mean, things. (Mgh, Sgh, TA.)

definition: , (S, A, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. salobN (S, K) and salabN , (K,) from the former of which the pl. suluwbN has been formed, on the authority of hearsay, (El-Jurjánee, Msb in art. qSd ,) He seized it, or carried it off, by force; (S, A, K;) as also ↓ Astlbhu . (S, K.) You say, salabahu Al$~aYo'a , aor. , inf. n. salobN and salabN ; and A_iy~aAhu ↓ Astlbhu ; (M, TA;) He seized, or carried off, by force [ from him the thing; or he spoiled him, despoiled him, plundered him, or deprived him, of the thing ]. (TA.) And salabotuhu vawobahu , (Mgh, * Msb,) aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. salobN , (Mgh, Msb,) I took away from him his garment; (Mgh, * Msb;) as also ↓ Aslbthu [perhaps a mistranscription for ↓ Astlbthu , but another instance of the former of these two verbs, in a similar sense, occurs in what follows]: originally, salabotu vawoba zyadoK [ I took away the garment of Zeyd ]; but the verb has been made to have zyd for its object, and the vwb is postponed, and put in the accus. case as a specificative [though by rule the specificative should be indeterminate]; and it may be suppressed, [so that you may say simply, salabotuhu , meaning I took away from him what was upon him or with him, spoiled him, or plundered him, ] the meaning being understood. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence] one says also, salabahu fuw^aAdahu waEaqolahu (tropical:) [ He, or it, despoiled him, or deprived him, of his heart and his reason ], and ↓ Aslbhu . (A, TA.) [The latter one might think to be a mistranscription for ↓ Astlbhu were it not for an instance of the same verb before men- tioned, and for the fact that it is immediately followed in the A by wahuwa musolabu AlEaqoli : perhaps, however, musolab may be here a mistake for musolib .] ― -b3- And Ausolubo h`*ihi AlqaSabapa (assumed tropical:) Peel thou this cane, or reed. (TA.) ― -b4- [In grammar and logic, salobN is used to signify (assumed tropical:) Privation, or deprivation, in a general sense; and (assumed tropical:) negation; opposed to A_ivobaAtN and A_iyjaAbN .] -A2- salobN [as an inf. n. of which the verb (app. salaba ) is not mentioned] (assumed tropical:) The going, or journeying, lightly and quickly. (M, K.) Ru-beh says, qado qad~aHato mino salobihin~a salobaA qaAruwrapu AlEayoni faSaArato waqobaA (assumed tropical:) [ The black of the eye became depressed so that it became a hollow in consequence of their going with much lightness and quickness: salobaA , for salobFA , being an absolute complement to the inf. n. in salobihin~a ]. (M. [See also 7.]) -A3- saliba [or salibato , as appears from what follows], aor. , (assumed tropical:) He [or she ] put on black garments (K, TA) which women wear at assemblies for the purpose of mourning. (TA. [See also 5.])

definition: ― -b2- Spoil, plunder, or booty;
sourceDefinition: : see saliybN . ― -b2- Spoil, plunder, or booty; (TA;) what is seized, or carried off, by force, (M, Msb, K, TA,) from a man, of spoils, whatever it be; (TA;) comprising all the clothing that is upon the man; (Mgh, Msb, TA;) accord. to Lth and Az (Mgh) and the Bári'; (Msb;) or whatever one of two antagonists in war takes from the other, of the things upon him and with him, i. e. of clothes and weapons, and his beast: of the measure faEalN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN , i. e., (TA,) i. q. masoluwbN [used in the manner of a subst., or as an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant]: (Mgh, TA:) pl. A^asolaAbN . (M, A, Msb, K.) You say, A^axa*a salaba Alqatiyli [ He took the spoil of the slain man ], and A^asolaAba AlqatolaY [ the spoils of the slain men]. (A.) ― -b3- Also (assumed tropical:) The hide and shanks and paunch of a slaughtered animal. (K. [App. so called because given to the slaughterer, as though they were his spoil; or, in the case of an animal of the chase, to the dog or dogs: see the verses cited voce badanN .]) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) The peel, or rind, [or skin, ] of a cane, or reed, (K, TA,) and of a tree. (TA.) And [particularly] The bark, or rind, of a kind of tree (S, K) well known (S) in El-Yemen, of which ropes are made, (S, K,) and which is coarser and harder than the fibres of the Theban palm-tree: (S:) hence it is that a well-known kind of [thick] rope [made of the fibres of the common palm-tree] is called by the vulgar ↓ salabapN : (TA:) or the bark of a kind of tree of which are made [ baskets of the kind called ] silaAl : (Sh, TA:) there is a market called ↓ suwqu Als~al~aAbiyna in El-Medeeneh, (Sh, S, K, TA,) and in Mekkeh also, as being the market [of the sellers, or manufacturers, of what are made] of salab : (Sh, TA:) it is also [said to be] (K) a certain kind of tall tree, (M, K,) growing symmetrically, which is taken and laid beneath hot ashes ( yumal~u ) and then split asunder, whereupon there comes forth form it a white mu$aAqap [or coarse fibrous substance ] like [ the fibres of the palm-tree, called ] liyf ; and it is one of the best of the materials of which ropes are made: the n. un. is with p : (M:) and (M, K) AHn says, (M,) it is a certain plant (M, K) which grows in form like candles, except that it is larger and longer, and of which are made ropes of every sort: (M:) and (M, K) some say, (M,) it is the fibrous substance ( lyf ) of the Theban palm-tree, (M, K,) this Lth asserts it to be, (TA,) which is brought from Mekkeh, (M,) and Lth adds, and it is white; but Az says that Lth has erred respecting it: A'Obeyd says, I asked respecting it, and was told, it is not the fibrous substance of the Theban palm-tree, but is a kind of tree well known in El-Yemen, of which ropes are made: and some say that it is the xuwS [or leaves ] of the vamaAm [or panic grass ]: and this [says SM] is what is commonly known among us in El-Yemen: (TA:) [accord. to Forskål, (Flor. Aegypt. Arab., p. cx.) this name is applied in El-Yemen to a species of hyacinth, which he terms hyacinthus aporus. ] A poet says, (S,) namely, [Murrah] Ibn-Mahkán [El-Temeemee], (M,) fana$ona$a Aljiloda EanohaAwahoYa baArikapN kamaA tuna$oni$u kaf~aA faAtilK salabaA (S, M, *) i. e. And he stripped off quickly the skin [ from her, while she was lying upon her breast, like as the two hands of the twister of ropes strips off quickly the seleb ]: (S in art. n$ :) some read qaAtilK , meaning [by the word following it] “ what is seized, or carried off by force, from one slain: ” (M:) As read faAtilK , with f ; IAar, with q : Th says that the right reading is that of As. (S in the present art.)

(TA.) -A2- See also saliybN .
